clinicalPearls: A rare photodermatosis of childhood characterised by recurrent crops of tense vesicles on sun-exposed skin that heal with distinctive pox-like (varioliform) scars
The face and the dorsa of the hands are typically affected, and lesions are often preceded by burning or stinging after sun exposure
Ultraviolet A is usually the provoking waveband, and phototesting may reproduce the characteristic lesions
Classic hydroa vacciniforme is benign and tends to remit spontaneously by adolescence or early adult life
An important caveat is the hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder, an Epstein-Barr virus associated entity with a more aggressive course that can involve systemic features
Features that should raise concern for the lymphoproliferative form include facial oedema, severe scarring, ulceration, fever, lymphadenopathy and lesions on non-exposed skin
Management centres on strict photoprotection, while atypical, severe or systemic disease requires investigation for Epstein-Barr virus and specialist haemato-oncological assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Classic hydroa vacciniforme is a poorly understood photodermatosis in which ultraviolet radiation, chiefly ultraviolet A, provokes epidermal necrosis and a vesicular, scarring reaction in sun-exposed skin, presumed to reflect an abnormal cutaneous response to ultraviolet-induced injury. In contrast, the hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder is a distinct Epstein-Barr virus driven proliferation of T or natural killer cells, in which the virus infects lymphocytes that infiltrate the skin and can behave in a locally aggressive or systemic manner. Distinguishing the benign photodermatosis from the virus-associated lymphoproliferative process is therefore central to management.
additionalDifferentials: Porphyria cutanea tarda and other blistering porphyrias
Bullous impetigo or other vesicular infection
additionalInvestigations: Phototesting to reproduce lesions and confirm ultraviolet A sensitivity
Skin biopsy showing epidermal necrosis, with immunophenotyping and Epstein-Barr virus studies where lymphoproliferative disease is suspected
Epstein-Barr virus serology and viral load testing in atypical or severe cases
Plasma, urine and faecal porphyrins to exclude erythropoietic protoporphyria
Full blood count and assessment for systemic involvement when the lymphoproliferative variant is considered
Antinuclear antibody testing where lupus is a differential
redFlags: Facial swelling, deep ulceration or unusually severe scarring suggesting the lymphoproliferative variant
Systemic features such as fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy
Marked burning or pain on exposure raising the possibility of erythropoietic protoporphyria
reference.prognosis: Classic hydroa vacciniforme usually follows a benign course with spontaneous improvement by adolescence, although some scarring may remain; by contrast, the Epstein-Barr virus associated hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder carries a more guarded prognosis and requires close specialist monitoring for progression to systemic disease.
pitfalls: Assuming all cases are benign and missing an underlying Epstein-Barr virus associated lymphoproliferative disorder
Confusing the vesicles with erythropoietic protoporphyria, in which scarring is usually subtler and porphyrins are abnormal
Failing to biopsy atypical or systemic disease, delaying recognition of the lymphoproliferative form
Overlooking the need for long-term follow-up in patients with severe or persistent lesions
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on the idiopathic photodermatoses
